title: The Ark, a Cart, and a Death
overview: David leads all Israel in bringing the ark, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence, toward Jerusalem, but the joyful procession stops when a man named Uzzah touches it and dies.

parts.label: David proposes bringing the ark (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The ark was a gold-covered chest holding the stone tablets of the law, and it had sat largely ignored in a village while Saul was king. David asks his leaders and the whole people to agree rather than simply ordering it, and everyone says yes.

parts.label: The nation gathers (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: People come from the far south near Egypt to the far north, so this is meant as an act of the whole nation. The ark was pictured as God's throne, with God seated above the winged figures called cherubim carved on its lid.

parts.label: A joyful procession on a cart (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: They load the ark onto a new ox cart, the way the Philistines had once sent it back, and celebrate with loud music. But Israel's law said the Levites, the tribe put in charge of the sacred objects, were to carry it on poles, and a later chapter says this mistake mattered (15:13).

parts.label: Uzzah dies (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: When the oxen stumble, Uzzah grabs the ark to steady it, and the text says the LORD struck him dead for touching it. David is angry about it too, and the place is named Perez Uzzah, meaning "outburst against Uzzah."

parts.label: The ark stays with Obed-Edom (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Now afraid, David leaves the ark with Obed-Edom, called a Gittite, which may mean he came from the Philistine city of Gath or from a Levite town with a similar name; scholars are unsure. For three months the LORD blesses his household, which many readers take to show that the same holy presence could bring good as well as danger.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand Uzzah's death: some see it as a just and necessary lesson about God's holiness, while others see it as reflecting an ancient understanding of the sacred that is hard to square with a God of mercy.
think: When someone means well but breaks a rule that others treat as sacred, how much should their good intentions count?
